<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is the most useful document in the series so far. It answers several open questions with better data: log-measured hours, a 24-month horizon, a registered mediation test, and a control-group comparison for waiting times. It is also candid about the Halden subset being an upper bound. Most of its rebuttals of the earlier papers are fair.

The main weaknesses are in the mediation analysis, which is presented as stronger confirmation than it can be, and in a few inconsistencies involving the hours measure and the control group.

## The core numbers check out

- **Per-hour gains at 24 months:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%**.
  - System logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%**.
- **Halden continuers:**
  - Hours: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of **13.4%**.
  - Per-hour gain: 96.8 / 86.6 = **+11.8%**.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter-arm cost:** restoring output after an 11.4% loss needs about 13% more staff, so the 12% figure is plausible. A 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is about three-quarters of cost; that assumption should be stated.

## Main issues

**1. The registered mediation test is not an independent confirmation.**
The test was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results showed the meetings correlation (r = 0.71). It was then run on the **same seven treated offices**. That makes it a pre-specified re-test of a hypothesis generated from those offices, not a replication. Three further problems:

- **Overlapping data.** If the 24-month difference-in-differences window includes months 1–11, part of the "confirmatory" data had already been seen when the hypothesis was registered. The cleanest test would use months 12–24 only.
- **The sample is still 14 offices.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information available. Office-months within an office are not independent.
- **The mediator path is observational.** Hours were randomised; meeting cuts were not. Offices with stronger managers may have cut meetings *and* improved productivity for other reasons. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's word "confirms" doesn't. "Is consistent with" is the defensible phrasing, and the method for the mediation confidence intervals with 14 clusters should be stated.

This doesn't mean the meetings hypothesis is wrong. The evidence for it has improved, and the baseline meeting data now resolve my earlier concern about balance: 7.4 v 7.2 hours at baseline. But Varga & Holm's specific objection, that the hypothesis was fitted to these seven offices, still applies. It needs testing in a different sample.

**2. How do system logs treat meeting time?**
Logs are described as recording time "working on cases." If they capture only case work and exclude meetings, the numbers don't fit together:

| | Baseline | Month 24 |
|---|---|---|
| Treated timesheet hours | ~37.9 | ~33.4 (−12%) |
| Recurring meetings | 7.4 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting time | ~30.5 | ~29.5 (−3%) |

On that reading, case-work hours should have fallen by about 3%, not the 11% the logs show.

If the logs do include meeting time, they are a measure of total time worked, and the comparison with timesheets is fine. In that case, how does cutting meetings raise output per *case-working* hour? The paper should define exactly what log time includes, because both the headline +8.5% and the mediation outcome depend on it.

**3. The control group was contaminated, and the meeting figures for it don't add up.**
Two control offices cut their own meetings in month 15. This matters in two ways:

- **Bias toward zero.** It narrows the treatment–control contrast in months 15–24 and biases the 24-month estimate downward. The paper should say how this was handled, for example with a sensitivity analysis that excludes or separately models those offices.
- **Arithmetic.** If two of seven control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, that alone lowers the control mean by about 0.6 hours. The control mean is reported to fall by only 0.2 (7.2 to 7.0). The other five offices must therefore have risen by about 0.5 hours each, or the month-24 figure was measured before the audit took effect. This needs explaining.

**4. The Summary measures the decline in an inconsistent way.**
The Summary describes a fall "from 12.5% to 8.5%," which compares timesheet hours at nine months with log hours at 24 months. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% to 9.8%**, about a 21% relative decline on the log scale. Section 5's "about a quarter" falls between the two versions. Using the timesheet comparison for the decline and reporting 8.5% as the stricter current level would be clearer.

The decline itself hasn't been tested. The intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily, so the data can't yet distinguish real fading from noise. Report a test of the 9-versus-24-month difference, ideally with wild-cluster bootstrap inference given seven offices per arm, as raised for the nine-month report.

## Secondary issues

- **The Halden reversions aren't all coverage-related.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The hospitality group and retail chain fit the coverage-bound pattern. The marketing agency cited client deadlines, and would presumably have been coded as discretionary work. One reversion in discretionary work is useful information, so it should be reported as such rather than folded into the coverage story.
- **The Halden baseline may be the wrong one.** The baseline of exactly 40.3 hours matches Varga & Holm's 27-organisation average. The 17-organisation subset averaged 40.4. Please confirm that 40.3 is these 11 organisations' own baseline, not a borrowed figure.
- **The Halden subset is filtered even more than stated.** These organisations completed the pilot, had submitted records, agreed to the follow-up (14 of 23), and chose to continue. "Survivors twice over" understates the filtering. It is still rightly presented as an upper bound.
- **Authors are assessing critiques of their own work.** Okafor co-authored the Halden working paper, and the Varden authors proposed the meetings hypothesis. Section 5 rules on critiques of both. This should be disclosed in a competing-interests statement, and it strengthens the case for independent replication.
- **Some outcomes still lack uncertainty measures.** Sick days and resignations have no intervals, as at nine months.

## The rebuttals in Section 5 are largely fair

**Against Varga & Holm:** the Varden data now meet every standard the re-analysis recommended: record-based output, actual hours, randomisation, no attrition, and follow-up beyond 18 months. They still show a gain. "Entirely an artifact" is no longer tenable.

Two points in the re-analysis's favour should be acknowledged more explicitly:
- The gain did decline, so it was partly right about the direction of change.
- Up to half the gain may come from reorganisation rather than shorter hours. That doesn't make the gain an artifact, but it does weaken the claim that *reduced hours* cause it.

**Against the meta-analysis:** the finding that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the concern that the "no decay" conclusion came from biased studies. That claim should be withdrawn.

## Where things now stand

| Question | Current best answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | ~8–10% at 24 months (Varden, log hours) | Moderate: one employer, 14 offices |
| Durability | Declined by about a fifth from 9 to 24 months; not yet tested statistically | Low–moderate |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall; the county ended the arm | High |
| Mechanism | Meetings plausibly a major pathway; fatigue smaller | Low: same offices, observational mediator path |
| Is the gain available without cutting hours? | Hinted at by two control offices | Very low |

The obvious next study is a trial with a **"reorganise without reducing hours" arm**: meeting audits and focus time at 37.5 hours, compared against reduced hours and against no change. That design would separate the hours effect from the reorganisation effect. The authors identify this question, but none of the existing studies can answer it.

I can draft a referee report, a competing-interests note, or a design sketch for the three-arm trial if any of those would help.
